items.title: TRICARE authorizes temporary prescription refill waivers for Mason County, West Virginia, due to severe weather
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries in Mason County, West Virginia, may receive emergency prescription refills now through Sept. 28, due to severe weather.
items.body:
Defense Health Agency Media Advisory

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 18, 2026

TRICARE authorizes temporary prescription refill waivers for Mason County, West Virginia, due to severe weather FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries in Mason County, West Virgina, may receive emergency prescription refills now through Sept. 28, due to severe weather.

To receive an emergency refill of prescription medications, TRICARE beneficiaries should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy. If the bottle is unavailable or the label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts, Inc., or their retail network pharmacy for assistance.

To find a network pharmacy, beneficiaries may call Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303, or search the https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/find-pharmacy.

If possible, visit the pharmacy where the prescription was filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may be filled at another store in that chain. If the clinician who prescribed the medication is available, beneficiaries can ask them to call in a new prescription to any network pharmacy.

As a reminder, TRICARE beneficiaries, other than active duty service members, may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider and do not need a referral. This allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency care for illnesses or injuries if their primary care provider is unavailable because of emergencies. Any TRICARE beneficiary who reasonably believes they have an emergency should always call 911 or, go to the nearest emergency room.

Beneficiaries are advised to visit Express Scripts’ https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/notices/weather/2026-sep-18/state-emergency-alert-severe-weather-west-virginia for updates.

###

The Defense Health Agency provides health services to 9.5 million beneficiaries, including uniformed service members, military retirees, and their families. The DHA operates one of the nation’s largest health plans, the TRICARE Health Plan, and manages a global network of more than 700 military hospitals, clinics, and dental facilities.

items.title: 130th Airlift Wing tests Agile Combat Employment during Operation Northern Vigilance
items.author: SMSgt Eugene Crist
items.summary: To prepare for the future fight, the 130th Airlift Wing, based out of McLaughlin Air National Guard Base, West Virginia, successfully executed split-site operations during Operation Northern Vigilance, Sept. 14-20. The full-scale readiness exercise tested the wing’s ability to employ Agile Combat Employment (ACE) concepts by operating a forward-deployed element here in Michigan while maintaining command and control (C2) from the Wing Operations Center in Charleston.
items.body: To prepare for the future fight, the 130th Airlift Wing, based out of McLaughlin Air National Guard Base, West Virginia, successfully executed split-site operations during Operation Northern Vigilance, Sept. 14-20. The full-scale readiness exercise tested the wing’s ability to employ Agile Combat Employment (ACE) concepts by operating a forward-deployed element here in Michigan while maintaining command and control (C2) from the Wing Operations Center in Charleston. "We wanted to ensure every unit got exactly what they needed out of this exercise, so we empowered the squadrons to drive their own tactical objectives," said Lt. Col. Robert Mills, 130th Mission Support Group deputy commander and forward element exercise commander. "Balancing those specialized, unit-level goals with our broader wing-wide priorities — such as completing physical fitness assessments and unmanned aircraft systems awareness training — ensures our Airmen are tactically, physically and mentally prepared for the modern threat landscape." A major focus of preparing for that modern threat landscape involved comprehensive unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) training. Beyond classroom instruction focused on threat awareness and counter-UAS strategies, Airmen faced the evolving hazard firsthand. The exercise's white cell deployed actual drones over the forward location to simulate ordnance-carrying enemy UASs, forcing personnel to quickly identify the threat, sound the alarm and execute immediate base defense and cover procedures during mock attacks. In addition to these tactical events, the unit capitalized on the off-station time to conduct annual physical fitness assessments. Administering PT tests during the temporary deployment allowed dozens of Airmen to fulfill their fundamental readiness requirements while proving the wing can sustain standard administrative functions even when operating in an austere, forward environment. Throughout the week, the forward element operated under a simulated contested, degraded and operationally limited environment. These exercise injects pushed Airmen to their limits, forcing them to step outside their primary career fields to respond to threats and sustain operations. "Compared to a traditional drill, I went from fixing printers and laptops to firing a weapon and experiencing what Security Forces goes through," said Staff Sgt. Gabe Garrison, a member of the 130th Communications Flight. "It has genuinely been a useful experience. It's the kind of training we wouldn't get any other time, and I'm just elated with the opportunity." Logistics, medical and maintenance personnel also faced high-pressure scenarios requiring rapid problem-solving and cross-utilization of skills to keep aircraft flying and personnel safe. "It’s been great being out here and seeing what the other maintainers do, since we don't interact with the other shops as much during a normal drill," said Airman 1st Class Solomon Stoll, an avionics technician with the 130th Maintenance Group. "As an avionics tech, I’ve been working with crew chiefs. It is really neat getting to see the Multi-Capable Airman concept in action." The wing's adaptability was put to the ultimate test when a real-world emergency interrupted the training environment. An F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the Texas Air National Guard's 149th Fighter Wing crashed in Traverse City, Michigan. While the pilot fortunately ejected safely, defenders from the 130th Security Forces Squadron operating out of the training center rapidly pivoted from the exercise to provide critical security and site control at the actual crash scene. "The true measure of this exercise's success isn't just in the planning, but in the incredible flexibility our Airmen showed on the ground," said Col. Chris Croson, 130th Mission Support Group commander and exercise evaluator. "Whether they were dealing with simulated contested scenarios or pivoting to handle real-world events, our Airmen seamlessly adapted at every turn. I could not be more proud of how the 130th AW executed this mission and proved our capability to fight and win from anywhere." By successfully establishing and sustaining the forward location before safely redeploying to West Virginia, the 130th AW proved its ability to rapidly project power, ensuring its Airmen remain ready to answer the nation's call anywhere, at any time.

items.title: Military Appreciation Night connects Morris Knolls community, Picatinny Arsenal
items.author: Eric Kowal
items.summary: ROCKAWAY, N.J. - Morris Knolls High School hosted a Military Appreciation Night during its varsity football game on Friday, Sept. 18, bringing together students, families, community members and local military representatives to recognize the service and contributions of the nation’s military personnel.
items.body: ROCKAWAY, N.J. - Morris Knolls High School hosted a Military Appreciation Night during its varsity football game on Friday, Sept. 18, bringing together students, families, community members and local military representatives to recognize the service and contributions of the nation’s military personnel. Prior to kickoff, the Morris Knolls ‘Golden Eagles’ ran on to the field carrying the nation’s colors and flags representing each brand of the U.S. Armed Forces, followed by the singing of the national anthem, a moment of silence, and honors to all military Veterans in attendance. The evening featured participation from Picatinny Arsenal, whose Garrison Commander Lt. Col. John Meier, took part in the pregame festivities by conducting the ceremonial coin toss using a military challenge coin provided by the installation’s commanding general, Maj. Gen. Christopher D. Schneider. Commanders and senior leaders often present coins to recognize exceptional performance, professionalism, leadership, or contributions. The ceremonial toss provided a meaningful connection between the local military community and the high school football program, incorporating a military tradition into the evening’s athletic activities. Picatinny Arsenal also supported the event by providing military equipment for static displays, giving attendees an opportunity to get an up-close look at some of the equipment associated with the installation’s mission. A team of employees representing the Arsenal’s U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center brought a M777A2 howitzer with 3D printed projectiles for the community to explore, while others provided training on a remotely operated weapons system known as CROWS that allows Soldiers to observe, aim, and engage targets from inside an armored vehicle. Local military recruiters representing the U.S. Army and U.S. Marine Corps were also on hand, supporting the appreciation night with informational and interactive displays. Their participation provided students and community members with opportunities to learn more about military service, career paths and the opportunities available through military service. Morris Knolls’ ‘Golden Eagles’ secured the win against the visiting Morristown ‘Colonials’ in the home conference matchup, delivering a strong performance on the gridiron as both teams continued their 2026 high school football campaigns. While the Golden Eagles entered the second half with a dominating 41-0 score, they were unable to tack any additional points, and the Colonials cut the lead with two touchdowns. The game’s final score was 41-13.

items.title: Illinois Army National Guard Promotes Macomb Native to Lieutenant Colonel
items.author: CPL Justin Malone
items.summary: The Illinois Army National Guard promoted Maj. Phyllida “Phyl” Shoudel to lieutenant colonel Sept. 19, 2026, at Camp Lincoln in Springfield, Illinois. Col. Michael Barton presided over the ceremony as Shoudel’s husband and two daughters pinned on her new rank. Shoudel thanked the family, mentors, peers and Soldiers who supported her throughout more than 18 years of service.
items.body: SPRINGFIELD, Ill. – Three sets of hands fastened the silver oak leaf to Maj. Phyllida “Phyl” Shoudel’s uniform Sept. 19 — her husband’s and her two daughters’ — as the Illinois Army National Guard promoted her to lieutenant colonel at the Illinois Military Academy Auditorium at Camp Lincoln. Col. Michael Barton, the Illinois Army National Guard state personnel officer (G-1), presided over the ceremony and said the room mattered as much as the rank. “Nothing gives me more joy as a leader than when you’re able to recognize one of your own and see someone advance,” Barton said. “And what makes it even more special is when you’re able to do it in front of family.” “No one earns a promotion alone,” Shoudel said, thanking the family, peers and mentors who supported her throughout her military career. During the ceremony, she dedicated a reading of the passage “The Measure of a Man” to honor the devotion, patience and character shown by those closest to her. “This promotion belongs to far more than the person wearing the rank,” she said. “It belongs to every mentor who invested in me … every soldier who trusted me and challenged me, and every friend who encouraged me along the way.” Shoudel, a resident of Macomb, serves as the G-1 operations officer for the Illinois Army National Guard. Her military career spans more than 18 years, beginning in 2008 when she joined the Illinois Army National Guard as a Simultaneous Membership Program cadet with the Western Illinois University ROTC program. She received her commission as an Adjutant General Corps officer in 2010. Addressing her parents, Jim and Charlene, who attended the ceremony, Shoudel said, “Thank you for raising me in a home where service wasn’t just respected. It was encouraged.” To her husband, she added, “You didn’t just support my career, you made it possible to reach this goal.” Shoudel also spoke directly to her daughters, Charlie, 6, and Frankie, 4, who moments earlier had helped pin the silver oak leaf to her uniform. “Charlie and Frankie may not fully understand yet what this promotion means,” she said. “I hope one day you’ll understand what it’s really about — it’s about commitment, it’s about honor, it’s about serving something greater than yourself. Your dad has taught you both to enjoy the ride along the way, and even though it takes unexpected turns, I hope you know I carry you with me every day.” Barton said the promotion carries weight beyond the insignia. “To make it to the rank of O5 is really a big deal,” he said. “With more rank comes more responsibility. But you’re ready for that, and that’s why you got selected to this position.” Throughout her career, Shoudel has served in numerous command and staff leadership assignments, including battalion personnel officer, battalion logistics officer, headquarters company commander, battalion operations officer, and executive officer at both the battalion and brigade levels within the 44th Chemical Battalion and the 404th Maneuver Enhancement Brigade. Her staff leadership also includes serving as battalion personnel officer for both the 198th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion and the 232nd Combat Sustainment Support Battalion, branch chief in the G-35 Force Integration Readiness Office, training officer for the 44th Chemical Battalion, and 65th Troop Command brigade S-1. From 2016 to 2017, Shoudel deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Freedom’s Sentinel. She served as the adjutant general for Bilateral Embedded Support Team (BEST) 18, advising the Afghan National Police 303rd Zone and Afghan National Army 203rd Corps at Advising Platform Lightning on human resources, human rights, and gender integration initiatives. Her military education includes the Adjutant General Basic Officer Leader Course, Chemical Captain’s Career Course, Chemical Defense Course, Master Resilience Trainer Course, Command and General Staff Officer Course, and the Advanced Operations Course. Shoudel holds a Bachelor of Arts in political science from Western Illinois University and a Master of Arts in human resources management from Webster University. Her awards and decorations include the Meritorious Service Medal, Army Commendation Medal with silver oak leaf cluster and combat “C” device, Army Achievement Medal, Afghanistan Campaign Medal, Order of the Combat Spur, and Order of the Dragon, alongside numerous state and federal recognitions. Several senior military leaders and distinguished guests also attended the ceremony, including Col. Paul Metzdorff, chief of staff of the Illinois Army National Guard; Brig. Gen. (ret.) Mark Alessia; and Shoudel’s mother-in-law, Karen. Shoudel resides in Macomb with her husband, Troy, a local law enforcement officer, their two daughters, Charlie, and Frankie, and their pets.

items.title: From liberation to legacy: Gavin helped build a lasting U.S.-Dutch bond in Nijmegen
items.author: SGT Griffin Payne
items.summary: NIJMEGEN, Netherlands — U.S. Army Maj. Gen. James M. Gavin arrived near Nijmegen in September 1944 commanding the 82nd Airborne Division during Operation Market Garden. After the fighting ended, he continued his relationship with the Dutch city and helped turn a connection forged during war into one centered on reconstruction, education and friendship.
items.body:
NIJMEGEN, Netherlands — U.S. Army Maj. Gen. James M. Gavin arrived near Nijmegen in September 1944 commanding the 82nd Airborne Division during Operation Market Garden. After the fighting ended, he continued his relationship with the Dutch city and helped turn a connection forged during war into one centered on reconstruction, education and friendship.

Allied forces launched Operation Market Garden Sept. 17, 1944, to secure critical bridges and terrain through the Netherlands. Gavin’s 82nd Airborne Division operated around Nijmegen and Groesbeek. On Sept. 20, paratroopers of the 504th Parachute Infantry Regiment crossed the Waal River with support from airborne engineers as Allied forces fought to capture Nijmegen’s bridges.

For Anja Adriaans, founder and chair of Friendship Albany Nijmegen, Gavin’s contribution to the city did not end with liberation. “General Gavin did two amazing things for the city of Nijmegen,” Adriaans said. “They liberated the city, and then they felt, well, we need to help. We want to help.”

Gavin returned to Nijmegen after the war and saw that liberation had only started the city’s long recovery. “Gavin came back in ’46 and ’47 after the liberation of our city, Nijmegen, and he said, ‘This city needs help,’” said Walter Hamers, Adriaans’ husband and an adviser to the FAN board.

Gavin looked across the Atlantic for help and found a natural connection in Albany, New York. Dutch settlers established Fort Orange in 1624 near what later became Albany, and that Dutch heritage gave Gavin a connection between the American city and Nijmegen. Residents throughout Albany joined the effort. Schools, churches, Scouts and civic organizations collected clothing, supplies and building materials for Nijmegen.

In 1947, Albany residents sent approximately 300 tons of aid to Nijmegen. The relief effort strengthened a connection between the cities that continues today. “That started a sister city connection,” Adriaans said.

Charlotte Brand, alderman of Nijmegen, said the people of Nijmegen faced another challenge after they gained their freedom. “Winning a war is one thing. Building peace is another,” Brand said. “Liberation can happen in a day. Reconstruction takes decades. And rebuilding a society takes even longer.”

Catholic University Nijmegen, now Radboud University, stood at the center of that reconstruction. The university opened in 1923 and endured years of occupation and war. In 1943, Rector Magnificus Bernard Hermesdorf refused to present students with a declaration of loyalty demanded by the German occupying authorities, and university leaders closed the institution rather than comply.

After the war, university leaders began rebuilding. Gavin supported that effort while he also helped connect Nijmegen with Albany. In 1946, supporters created the American Committee to Aid the University of Nijmegen to raise money and assistance for the university’s reconstruction, and historical records list Gavin among its members.

“After the war, he remained committed to Nijmegen,” Brand said. “He helped bring American support to our city, support that included food, clothing and building materials, but also support for the university and the rebuilding of our community.”

Adriaans said Gavin considered education an important part of Nijmegen’s recovery. “They wanted to help the University of Nijmegen to restore, and that is why General Gavin stepped in a committee to aid the Catholic University of Nijmegen,” Adriaans said.

Gavin also valued education for personal reasons. His daughter, Chloe Gavin, said her father’s own experiences shaped his desire to give other people opportunities to learn.

American veterans supported that goal. Money raised by American veterans contributed to the construction of the university’s medical faculty building, and supporters in the United States sent approximately 30,000 books to replenish the university library.

“One powerful example of that reconstruction is what is now Radboud University Medical Center,” Brand said. “It was building a future: a place for healthcare, education, and research, where new generations could learn, heal, and contribute to society.”

In 2026, Radboud University Medical Center marks 75 years of medical education and 70 years of academic hospital care. Bertine Lahuis, chair of the Executive Board of Radboud University Medical Center, connected those milestones to the opportunities that followed liberation. “The liberation created the conditions for rebuilding, for growth, and for investing in knowledge, healthcare and education,” Lahuis said.

Lahuis said the medical center provides a lasting example of what grew from that postwar cooperation. “After the liberation, the seeds were planted for a lasting friendship between Nijmegen and Albany,” Lahuis said. “The people of Albany made an important contribution to the reconstruction of our city, enabling the university to continue to grow and, ultimately, allowing the medical faculty and university hospital of the past to develop into the university medical center we are today.”

For local student Wesley Koster, the legacy of liberation remains visible in the opportunities students have today.

"Because of the liberation, we can study freely. During the war, our future looked dim. We are very thankful to live in freedom and have the opportunity to study," Koster said

A plaque inside Radboudumc commemorates the 82nd Airborne Division and its connection to the university. The memorial links the Soldiers who fought around Nijmegen with the institution that American veterans later helped support.

More than eight decades after Gavin arrived near Nijmegen as a Soldier, his connection to the city reaches far beyond the battlefield. Americans and Dutch citizens continue crossing the Atlantic, students continue learning from their shared history, and Radboud University Medical Center continues educating, researching and caring for patients.

Liberation brought Americans and the people of Nijmegen together. What they built afterward gave that relationship a future.

items.title: The F-117: Now Washington Can See Stealth in the Light of History
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: The Smithsonian’s announcement that an F-117A Nighthawk, tail number 85-0818, is headed to the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum, or NASM, is welcome news. The acquisition of this Nighthawk fills a long-standing historical gap—indeed, need—in the collections of what is generally considered the world’s premier air and space museum. The post The F-117: Now Washington Can See Stealth in the Light of History appeared first on Air &a
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Smithsonian’s announcement that an F-117A Nighthawk, tail number 85-0818, is headed to the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum , or NASM, is welcome news. Historically, 90 percent of all visitors to Washington D.C. go to the Smithsonian. Of those, 90 percent visit the NASM, either downtown or at its Dulles annex; some visit both. 85-0818 will be seen by millions.

The acquisition of this Nighthawk fills a long-standing historical gap—indeed, need—in the collections of what is generally considered the world’s premier air and space museum .

There are F-117As on exhibit at a few other military and aviation museums across the country (including at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Dayton, Ohio), but visitors to the NASM have not been able to see this truly transformational Air Force airplane.

Exposing the public to this history and sharing its story will help American taxpayers better understand what their hard-earned dollars do for our Air Force and, perhaps, inspire future generations who want to fly or design future generations of aircraft.

By doing so, the Air Force is sharing an important and little-known piece of its history with a broader audience.

Created by a small team working for Lockheed Skunk Works Chief Ben Rich, the F-117A is not just one more aging warbird cleaned up for exhibit. In practical terms, the F-117A began the “stealth” revolution that today includes aircraft, missiles, drones, and spacecraft, as well as treatments for ships at sea.

Some notable air weapons—Firebee reconnaissance drones in Vietnam, the Lockheed Blackbird strategic reconnaissance aircraft, and selected Cold War missiles—had stealthy features. But the F-117A was the world’s first aircraft designed from the outset with an unprecedentedly small radar cross section, a reduced infrared signature, and reduced noise and visual signatures. These attributes were made possible by its shape, radar-absorbent materials, radar-absorbent structures, and radar-absorbent edge-treatments and coatings.

Members of the design team recognized it was likely impossible to develop a truly invisible airplane—at least with the faceted technology of “first generation” stealth—but that if they could come up with a design that could frustrate search, tracking, and fire-control radars, they could design an airplane that would be only fleetingly and tantalizingly visible. Such a plane could not be tracked and would be virtually impossible to target except at very close range. Thus, its reflective signature characteristics took precedent over all other design criteria, a first in the history of aircraft design.

The F-117 was a product of the computer age, made possible by the galloping advances in computer prediction and command execution by Moore’s Law. Inherently unstable, its unique radar-defeating shape demanded computerized “fly-by-wire” flight control, as well. It incorporated a forward-looking infrared sensor and laser targeting attack system.

Though a product of the computer age, the roots of the F-117 went back to the Great War, when German and Allied designers tried to reduce the visual signature of early deep-penetration reconnaissance and bomber airplanes by incorporating see-through translucent coverings over their wooden structures, or complex camouflage schemes. Neither worked well.

Striking strategic targets behind enemy lines was likewise an early objective of airpower advocates all the way back to World War I. Later, deep strikes into Germany, Occupied Europe, and Japan helped the allies win World War II. But the achievements of early strategic bombing had to be weighed against heavy losses, which led to tens of thousands of dead, missing, and wounded aviators across multiple wars.

During the Cold War, advances in air defenses raised the price and risk of air combat. Sophisticated air defense fighters, new radar guided surface-to-air-missiles, and improved antiaircraft artillery—increasingly netted into ever-more-sophisticated command, control, communications and intelligence networks—began to gain the upper hand.

American aircraft losses in Vietnam from 1965-1973 (and Israeli losses in the October 1973 Arab-Israeli War) profoundly demonstrated that the ever-more-dangerous linkage of radar-cued SAMs and flak, coupled with infrared MANPADS and mobile antiaircraft systems, such as the notorious Soviet ZSU-23-4 Shilka, created a new and highly lethal air defense nexus.

By 1972-1973, these weapons were endangering third-generation aircraft, such as the then-new F-4E, and even threatening new fourth-generation combat aircraft, such as the F-14A, F-15A, F-16A, and F/A-18A, which were then in development.

In the final two weeks of Operation Linebacker II, in December 1972, the U.S. lost 27 planes over North Vietnam—including 15 B-52 bombers, the iconic backbone of America’s bomber force. The following year, in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Israel lost over a 100 aircraft in a single month—35 percent of its prewar aircraft.

Applying those loss rates to a potential Soviet assault through the Fulda Gap against NATO, American military leaders realized the U.S. Air Force would run out of planes in only about two weeks.

Something had to change. DARPA, the Air Force, and industry attacked the problem, inventing an aircraft unlike any previously seen. Ironically, DARPA’s choice of possible contenders for a low radar cross section signature design did not include Lockheed. But Ben Rich’s strenuous advocacy finally led to the inclusion of the Skunk Works, which ultimately won a “pole off” radar test range competition against Northrop. By 1977, Lockheed test pilots were secretly flying the experimental “Have Blue” against a variety of radar types, confirming it was nearly invisible to conventional radars. Though both “HB” demonstrators eventually crashed (one from a hard landing, and the other from an inflight fire—both pilots survived), these had nothing to do with stealth, and they provided vital lessons for the future.

Just four years later, Lockheed delivered the first F-117 Nighthawk . What Americans would come to know as “the Stealth Fighter” was roughly the size of an F-15A, with a flyaway cost of $42.6 million in then-year dollars. Nine years after that, in the summer of 1990, the USAF had a fleet of 59—just in time for Operation Desert Storm.

Operating in total secrecy from a specially constructed base at Tonopah in the Nevada desert, the F-117A and its mysterious parent unit, the 4450th Test Group, was among the nation’s biggest secrets. In 1983 it achieved initial operational capability, though further refinement and development of its signature GBU-27 hardened 2,000-lb laser-guided bomb took still more time. In 1988, in a move both to deter the Soviet Union and to address what were increasingly widespread calls for some information release, officials finally shared a grainy image of the aircraft with the public.

The Nighthawk’s first operational use over Panama against a military facility at Rio Hato during Operation Just Cause was a disappointment. Confusion over targeting from higher command and technical problems with the target designation system led to one airplane significantly missing its aim point. Perhaps predictably, after that, critics attempted to use the results to argue against the viability of stealth.

Yet in Desert Strom, the Airmen of the 37th Tactical Fighter Wing fully demonstrated the power of stealth. On Jan. 17, 1991, the opening night of Operation Desert Storm, 36 F-117s generated 42 attack sorties and struck roughly 31 percent of the coalition’s targets across the breadth and depth of Iraq—despite constituting just 2.5 percent of the strike force. They all returned safely home.

The attacks constituted a revolution in air warfare, evident by comparing what the F-117s did with a nonstealthy strike package launched that same night. To get to a single target, that strike package employed 41 planes—only eight of which dropped bombs. Without stealth, the eight bomb-carrying planes needed multiple escorts to jam air defense radars, suppress surface-to-air missile threats, and counter enemy fighters. In contrast, operating by themselves, every stealth fighter launched was a striker, capable of hitting two targets on a single sortie.

That night, stealth demonstrated unparalleled operational value. From a cost perspective, even though each individual F-117 was more expensive than conventional equivalents, stealth proved more efficient than conventional attack. The stealth strike package required no escort or supporting aircraft aside from refueling tankers and thus placed fewer aircrew in danger. Considering the cost of more planes, more aircrew, sustainment costs, logistical support, and basing requirements, the U.S. Air Force had permanently altered the rules of air combat.

Commanders prized the F-117s, which continued in heavy use in nearly every U.S. combat operation through Operation Iraqi Freedom. The Air Force retired the planes in 2008, putting them in protected storage at the secret base first constructed for their use in Tonopah, Nev.

By then, however, stealth aircraft had multiplied across the force. The F-117 paved the way for the stealthy B-2, F-22, F-35, RQ-170, and the next-generation B-21 and F-47. Today, newly designed semi-autonomous aircraft, known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft, and some high-end munitions also harness stealth characteristics.

The F-117 was the unique product of American innovation, an extraordinarily successful quick-turn acquisition program, with the first aircraft delivered in 1981 and IOC achieved in 1983. Many people from various organizations came together to make it a success, and it teaches what’s possible when government and industry innovators partner and collaborate on a well-defined challenge, using streamlined management, minimal bureaucracy, and a special access program approach.

Creating a flying stealth airplane was one thing; turning it into a devastating operational weapon system was quite another. Here the senior leaders, executives, planners, designers, builders, and others delivered when the chips were down. The F-117A at the Smithsonian will stand as a reminder and tribute to them and, in particular, to all those Air Force military and civilian senior leaders, engineers, test pilots, flight test engineers, test directors, planners, operational combat airmen, and maintainers working nationwide from the Pentagon to bases and remote test sites in the deserts of the great Southwest.

Among the most crucial lessons of the Stealth Fighter are ones we learned in its first real operational test: that just as airpower pioneers predicted, deep strike attack is both the sine qua non and the secret to victory. And in the modern era, only stealth makes that possible.

Sept. 20, 2026 | By Richard P. Hallion

History

Sept. 18, 2026

Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs, but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.

More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.

As the threat of Iranian-made drones grew, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them. The service fielded the new capability in roughly a week.

Sept. 17, 2026

When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly.

The Air Force’s new Collaborative Combat Aircraft will take part in their first large-force engagement exercise in December, the head of the drones’ Experimental Operations Unit said Sept. 15.

Sept. 16, 2026

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.

When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot. Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former F-15 and F-22 pilot, says that must change to help the Air Force get the resources it…

The new head of Air Mobility Command said Sept. 16 he wants to explore an unmanned option for the service’s next-generation aerial refueling system.

items.title: U.S. naval forces join eight nations in exercise to strengthen maritime security
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: U.S. naval forces joined maritime forces from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group (EWG) on Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity (MS JCA), Sept. 20.
items.body:
U.S. naval forces joined maritime forces from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group (EWG) on Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity (MS JCA), Sept. 20.

Co-hosted by Japan and the Republic of the Philippines, the ADMM-Plus is executing the MS JCA as a multilateral maritime exercise designed to foster cooperation, enhance collective maritime domain awareness, and strengthen regional resilience against natural disasters.

"We are honored to be operating alongside our allies and regional partners for the MS JCA," said U.S. Navy Capt. Bryan Gallant, operations officer for Commander, Task Force 76. "Practicing together now ensures we are ready before a crisis. This exercise builds the hands-on proficiency we need to coordinate smoothly and respond effectively to real-world challenges alongside our partners, keeping the Indo-Pacific free and open."

Participating nations actively deploying ships, aircraft, and personnel include Australia, Brunei, India, Japan, New Zealand, the Republic of the Philippines, the Republic of Singapore, and the United States.

U.S. Navy participation included Independence-variant littoral combat ship USS Canberra (LCS 30) and a P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and reconnaissance aircraft. Allied and partner nation vessels operating in the combined task group included Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Hyuga-class helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH 182); Indian Navy Shivalik-class stealth multi-role frigate INS Sahyadri (F49) and Kora-class corvette INS Kulish (P63); Philippines Navy Jose Rizal-class frigate BRP Jose Rizal (FFG14) and Tarlac-class landing platform dock BRP Tarlac (LD601); Royal Australian Navy Anzac-class frigate HMAS Perth (FFH 157); Republic of Singapore Navy Independence-class littoral mission vessel RSS Justice; Royal Brunei Navy Darussalam-class offshore patrol vessel KDB Darussalam (06); and Royal New Zealand Navy Anzac-class frigate HMNZS Te Mana (F 111) and Polar-class sustainment vessel HMNZS Aotearoa (A 11).

Following the opening ceremony, the shore phase of the exercise will occur in Subic Bay, Zambales, Philippines, and feature a disaster-response tabletop exercise, subject matter expertise exchanges, an open house aboard participating ships, and cultural exchanges. The exercise will include a follow-on sea phase where key maritime skillsets and interoperability will be trained by the participants.

The ADMM-Plus is a platform for ASEAN and its dialogue partners to strengthen security and defense cooperation for peace, stability, and development in the region. The inaugural ADMM-Plus was convened in Ha Noi, Vietnam, Oct. 12, 2010. The ADMM-Plus EWG coordinates the MS JCA, which is a maritime exercise focusing on enhancing multilateral interoperability, information sharing, and practical cooperation among participating nations' maritime forces to engage with a humanitarian assistance and disaster response scenario.

U.S. 7th Fleet, the Navy’s largest forward-deployed numbered fleet, routinely interacts and operates with allies and partners in preserving a free and open Indo-Pacific.

-END-

items.title: Joint Region Marianas recognizes 2025 Sister School-Sister Village Award winners
items.author: PO2 Janae McCoy
items.summary: TUMON, Guam (Sept. 20, 2026) — Joint Region Marianas recognized the winners of the 2025 Sister School-Sister Village Award during a ceremony at the USO Tumon Bay, Sept. 18.
items.body:
TUMON, Guam (Sept. 20, 2026) — Joint Region Marianas recognized the winners of the 2025 Sister School-Sister Village Award during a ceremony at the USO Tumon Bay, Sept. 18.

The Sister School-Sister Village program pairs military commands across Guam with local villages, schools and community organizations, encouraging service members and their families to build lasting relationships with the communities they call home.

This year’s nominees contributed tens of thousands of volunteer hours supporting classrooms, environmental cleanup efforts, youth mentorship, and other community initiatives across the island.

Rear Adm. Brett Mietus, commander, JRM, presented awards to the commands in the small, medium and large categories, respectively.

“I recently saw firsthand at Southern High School what happens when our service members answer a community’s call for help” said Mietus. “A campus is renewed, students see that they matter, and a partnership becomes real. That is what we recognize today. These commands did not simply log volunteer hours. They gave their time, talent and energy to strengthen the villages, schools and organizations that make Guam home. Their service reflects the very best of our joint force and our commitment to being trusted partners in this community.”

The 36th Wing, Andersen Air Force Base, received the Large Category award for a community-relations program involving more than 950 Airmen, Sailors and civilian personnel. Through partnerships with 19 villages, 11 schools and 14 nonprofit organizations, the wing supported initiatives ranging from the Liberation Day flyover, base tours for island youth and international cadets, and sustained support to programs such as Operation Christmas Drop and the Marine Turtle Patrol.

U.S. Naval Base Guam earned the Medium Category award after mobilizing 445 Sailors and civilians to support 11 villages and six schools. Volunteers assisted with Guam’s Homeless Point-in-Time Count, planted more than 1,000 trees along the Ugum River watershed and supported the annual Back to Sumay Day remembrance, which welcomes former Sumay residents and their descendants back to the area their families once called home.

Marine Corps Base Camp Blaz received the Small Category award. The installation established a formal community-relations program guided by a dedicated base order, with 53 percent of the command contributing nearly 1,800 volunteer hours during the year. Its partnerships included Finegayan Elementary School, the Dededo Mayor’s Office and a Toys for Tots campaign that supported children on Guam, Saipan, Tinian and Rota.

The winning commands’ efforts reflect the broader purpose of the program by building lasting relationships between the military and communities across Guam.

“The work recognized today reflects the commitment of our service members who to give back and it encourages them to continue building connections throughout Guam,” said Shaina O’Neal, Sister School-Sister Village program coordinator. “We are one island, and this program shows what can be accomplished through a One Guam mindset. Every act of kindness strengthens our community as a whole.”

Established in 1974, the Sister School-Sister Village program provided a lasting framework for military units to support Guam beyond their primary missions. The program expanded in 1987 to include adopt-a-school partnerships, building a tradition of service that continues today.

-30-

items.title: Delta Leadership Course bridges air and space
items.author: Jennifer Green-Lanchoney
items.summary: Space Launch Delta 30 recently hosted its inaugural Delta Leadership Course, equipping 13 commanders and senior enlisted leaders with the knowledge, relationships and resources necessary to lead Guardians and Airmen at a Space Force installation. The locally developed course supports the Department of the Air Force’s emphasis on preparing command teams to build ready units, uphold standards, care for their people and execute the mission in a rapidly changing operational environment.
items.body: VANDENBERG SPACE FORCE BASE, Calif. —Space Launch Delta 30 recently hosted its inaugural Delta Leadership Course, equipping 13 commanders and senior enlisted leaders with the knowledge, relationships and resources necessary to lead Guardians and Airmen at a Space Force installation. The locally developed course supports the Department of the Air Force’s emphasis on preparing command teams to build ready units, uphold standards, care for their people and execute the mission in a rapidly changing operational environment. For many of the participating Air Force leaders, an assignment at Vandenberg represents their first experience commanding within a Space Force-led installation. The weeklong course introduced them to Vandenberg’s mission, organizational structure, support network and distinct service culture while reinforcing the responsibilities shared by command teams across the Department of the Air Force. “As Delta Commanders, our responsibility is to ensure our Squadron Commanders have the tools, context and relationships they need to take care of their people and accomplish the mission,” said U.S. Space Force Col. James T. Horne III, SLD 30 commander. “At Vandenberg, that also means understanding how Guardians and Airmen work together to enable launch, test and aeronautical operations essential to our nation’s security.” Recognizing the challenges and opportunities of command teams at Vandenberg, U.S. Air Force Col. Lawrence A. Smith II, SLD 30 deputy commander, conceptualized a tailored leadership program. With Horne’s full backing and direction to move forward, Smith turned the concept into an actionable curriculum to prepare newly assigned leaders. “We recognized there was an opportunity to better prepare command teams for the unique experience of leading at a Space Force installation,” said Smith. “Drawing from proven Air Force practices, our team built a course specifically for Vandenberg’s mission and the Airmen and Guardians who execute it. What began as a local solution may ultimately offer a useful model for how the Space Force welcomes and equips command teams across the service.” The curriculum brought several command teams together for an integrated look at what it takes to lead effectively at the Department of the Air Force’s fastest-growing space launch delta. “This was an opportunity to create something completely new for the Space Force while drawing on proven Air Force leadership practices,” said U.S. Air Force ChiefMaster Sgt. Joshua Sanders, SLD 30 senior enlisted Airman. “Because I was also new to Vandenberg, I could bring the questions and challenges incoming command teams experience directly into the development process. We built a course that connects those established practices with the unique mission, culture and support structure of a Space Force installation.” The course connected participants with installation leaders, mission partners and helping agencies responsible for readiness, personnel development and family support. Topics included command authorities and responsibilities, standards and accountability, talent management, installation operations, quality of life, family readiness and resources specific to Vandenberg SFBfor Guardians and Airmen. “Our people are our greatest resource, but taking care of them requires more than knowing what programs are available,” said U.S. Space Force Chief Master Sgt. Shannan Sanchez, Command senior enlisted leader. “Leaders must understand the Space Force mission; the Guardian experience and the different perspectives Airmen bring to this installation. This course gives command teams the context and relationships to lead both services effectively, uphold standards and make informed decisions that strengthen their people, their units and our collective readiness.” SLD 30 supports military, civil and commercial space launch, missile testing and aeronautical operations and its mission has grown more than 1300% in the last five years. The program addressed the experiences of Airmen assigned to a Space Force base and the responsibilities leaders have in helping both Guardians and Airmen navigate an exponentially growing service environment. The course emphasized the partnership between commanders and senior enlisted leaders and the importance of approaching leadership as an integrated team. It also allowed participants to establish relationships across organizational boundaries, share experiences and identify common challenges before those challenges affect personnel or mission execution. By understanding the cultures, missions and needs of both services, command teams are better positioned to strengthen unit cohesion and ensure every member remains connected to the mission. “This course helped connect the dots—what’s expected of us as commanders, how Vandenberg operates and where to turn when our people need support,” said U.S. Air Force Maj. Joanne Whitlock, SLD 30 Logistics and Readiness Squadron commander. “I’m leaving this course better prepared to set clear expectations, take care of my Airmen, and keep the team focused on the mission.” The inaugural Delta Leadership Course establishes a locally developed framework that can evolve alongside Vandenberg’s mission and workforce. Participant feedback will be used to strengthen future iterations of the annual program. “The course did an outstanding job highlighting some blind spots we didn’t know we had,” said U.S. Space Force Master Sgt. Jeffrey Wynn, 30th Operations Support Squadron senior enlisted leader. “The course should be made available to a wider population.” Ultimately, the course reflects a fundamental readiness principle: Command teams that understand their mission, know their people and can connect them with the right resources are better prepared to lead through change and deliver combat capability.

items.title: Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs, but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight. The post Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs—aircraft can stay in depot for weeks and months getting repairs—but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.

As the war with Iran stretched from its projected timeline of weeks into several months, Air Force leaders were forced to adapt its aircraft maintenance strategy for a prolonged conflict.

The service relies on three maintenance depots at Hill Air Force Base, Utah; Robins Air Force Base, Ga.; and Tinker Air Force Base, Okla.—to conduct major maintenance overhauls and inspections on fighters, bombers, airlifters, and other aircraft.

During Epic Fury, barrages of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. forces operating out of Middle East resulted in levels of battle damage that normally would have required the aircraft to be transported back stateside for repairs.

Instead, Air Force Materiel Command temporarily surged a depot capability to RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom so damaged aircraft could be patched up and sent back into combat, AFMC Commander Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry told an audience this week at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber conference .

“Most people think of depots as Tinker, Robbins, and Hill; well, it doesn’t need to be just there,” Hurry said. “We knew you needed a capability out at Mildenhall … what if we push that forward?”

“That’s what we’ve been asking all of our Airmen—how do we do things smarter? How do we deliver capability faster? It doesn’t have to be 7,000 miles away.”

Air Mobility Command’s new boss, Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, said Hurry’s move paid off, describing how the depot operation quickly repaired damaged aerial refueling booms on KC-135 Stratotanker s.

“I think we turned 30 [booms] instead of bringing them all the way back to the states,” Tulley said, adding it was a great example of “generating readiness in contact.”

Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach made readiness a defining priority soon after taking their jobs last year. The intense pace of operations against Iran will stress that focus, with much of the fleet likely to need heavy maintenance overhauls to reset.

The Air Force’s proposed 2027 budget includes $4.2 billion for the Consolidated Sustainment Activity Group, which is responsible for managing spare parts.

“We absolutely need additional funding for spares,” Hurry said, adding “right now , we have a $14 billion hole in supply.”

“I know we’re not going to get it all at once, … but once we get even a penny, we have to be ready to execute it,” Hurry said. That will mean securing long-term contracts to inject stability into the supply chain.

“The other thing is, we’re looking for is multiple sources of supply; gone are the days of monopolies. We can’t just have one person producing the one critical part,” Hurry said. “I need five of you producing them because if we get down to the crunch, we’re going to have to have a healthy shelf so that we can fight globally.”

Meanwhile, Hurry said AFMC has started using artificial intelligence tools to improve forecasting accuracy. “We’re using all sorts of things to try to make sure we better understand where the needs are and where we can position those critical assets globally around the world,” she said.

Additive manufacturing is another tool AFMC has started to use to “reverse engineer some of the parts that we need,” she added.

But technology alone isn’t enough, she said, adding that “process improvement” can solve a lot of challenges.

“Quite frankly, if we can understand the process and break it down into constraint and mitigate that constrain, the collective throughput of the entire system goes so much better,” Hurry said. “That’s exactly what’s going on in the depot. That’s exactly what we did when we surged operations for [Epic Fury].”

items.title: Air Force Retires EC-130H, Embraces EA-37B, as Davis-Monthan Transitions
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there retired its final A-10 Warthog, another major transition for the base. The post Air Force Retires EC-130H, Embraces EA-37B, as Davis-Monthan Transitions appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there inactivated its A-10 Warthog units, another major transition for the base.

The Compass Call mission is transitioning from the old propeller-driven EC-130s to the sleek EA-37B , which packs the electronic warfare mission into a modified Gulfstream 550 jet. The 55th Electronic Combat Group at Davis-Monthan has five of the new jets on hand, en route to a planned dozen by 2028 and 22 by 2031.

Meanwhile, the 355th is transitioning to a rescue mission as the base prepares to host a new special operations wing.

The new Compass Call jets compress the targeting, jamming, and other electronic warfare missions into a tighter space. About 70 percent of the equipment is unchanged, but instead of 13 Airmen performing Compass Call functions in the EC-130H, the E-37 B needs only nine.

“Its ‘plug-and-play’ architecture allows for rapid software updates and the integration of new capabilities to counter emerging threats and technologies without costly redesigns,” Maj. Claire Fitle, 355th Wing spokesperson, told Air & Space Forces Magazine by email.

The jet has “significantly increased speed, altitude, and range compared with the legacy EC-130H,” Fitle wrote. The equipment can also detect and jam a wider range of enemy systems from farther distances.

The new system is software-driven, allowing rapid updates via software rather than hardware modifications, “dramatically reducing response time … [to] evolving electromagnetic threats,” Fitle wrote.

Decade-long Road to Upgrade

The Air Force began seeking a replacement for the EC-130H in 2014, then awarded L3 Technologies a contract in 2017 to engineer the capability into a smaller airframe. Congress sped up the procurement program two years later, originally expecting to complete procurement in 2026.

The first five aircraft lack some low-band capability, which is anticipated in the remaining aircraft.

BAE Systems and L3Harris delivered the first EA-37B for developmental testing in 2023 , and Air Combat Command received the first two airframes in 2024 . Initial training sorties began in 2025 and operational testing wrapped up within the year. Contractors will be primarily responsible for maintaining the EA-37Bs at Davis-Monthan, Fitle wrote.

During Operation Epic Fury, they got their first combat exposure —even before the Air Force declared full operational capability.

The EC-130H saw combat action during Operation Just Cause in Panama, 1989, Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Operation Allied Force in Kosovo in 1999, and throughout the Global War on Terror in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria over the past 25 years. It was a workhorse to the end, making its final mission in the early stages of Operation Epic Fury.

The first legacy EC-130H retired in 2021, while the last aircraft conducted its final flight Sept. 2.

The 355th, 492nd, and the A-10

In a parallel event, the 355th inactivated its A-10 Warthog units as well Sept. 18. While the larger Air Force is keeping the popular close air support platform around until the 2030s, the 355th is becoming a “rescue hub,” Fitle wrote.

“Close air support is an enduring mission rather than a single airframe, and the Air Force will continue providing responsive CAS across the joint battlespace through a flexible mix of fifth- and fourth-generation multirole aircraft,” she wrote. “Experienced A-10 aircrew and maintainers are transitioning their close-support expertise directly into these platforms to ensure seamless coverage.”

The wing will continue its CSAR and personnel recovery mission through the 563rd Rescue Group using the HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopter and the HC-130J Combat King II aircraft.

Meanwhile, the 492nd Special Operations Wing is moving to Davis-Monthan, with full operational capability expected between 2028-29. The move comes as the USAF has restructured the former training wing.

The special ops wing will backfill the 355th’s A-10 capabilities by basing its OA-1K Skyraider II and CV-22 Osprey s at Davis-Monthan as well, expanding strike and specialized operational capabilities.

The former “high-end” strike missions will be absorbed by fifth-generation aircraft across USAF.

items.title: Now Back in Uniform: At Least 134 Airmen, Guardians Who Refused COVID Vaccine
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said. The post Now Back in Uniform: At Least 134 Airmen, Guardians Who Refused COVID Vaccine appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.

Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs Richard Anderson said that, as of Sept. 15, 137 individuals have applied for reinstatement so far, and 48 have been accepted. Another 86 have returned through the reaccession process, for a total of 134 service members have already rejoined the ranks.

The two routes back are distinct: Reinstatement is slower, requiring interested veterans to apply to the Air Force Board for Correction of Military Records. If successful, the payoff is they will be eligible for back pay and other benefits—offset by whatever they earned in civilian jobs while separated. Reaccession, which is faster, skips the board process but also does not include back pay. A third option is to go through reaccession and only then apply for reinstatement after they have rejoined the ranks.

The Air Force and Space Force involuntarily separated about 600 Airmen and Guardsians for refusing the COVID shot: then-Undersecretary of the Air Force Gina Ortiz Jones pegged the number at 610 in early 2023 , and the Air Force Review Boards Agency said it identified 595 cases in a review earlier this year.

But others chose to leave when their service commitment was up rather than be vaccinated, and they are eligible to rejoin as well. Thousands of Airmen and Guardians sought medical and religious exemptions and refused the mandatory shots in 2021 and 2022. But the number that left voluntarily before the mandate was lifted in early 2023 is unclear.

Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the Pentagon has made a concerted effort to make good on a campaign promise to restore those to service who departed because of the mandate, which was ordered by then-Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin. Current Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April 2025 that his department was “welcoming actively back those warriors of conscience.”

Since then, the Pentagon has extended the deadline for applying until April 2027, and has reduced the minimum service obligation for those returning from four years to two.

Anderson and his team have also taken steps to ease the process for those who wish to return. In August, they announced medical processing and board reviews would take place simultaneously to speed the reinstatement process, and they hired case managers to help those seeking to return to service.

“We now, I think, have stabilized criteria and expectations,” Anderson said. “We have done a very sustained comms program to tell the affected universe that they are welcome back and welcome to apply … and we’ll continue to to advertise very heavily to get worthy Airmen and Guardians back in uniform.”

According to statistics compiled by the Department of the Air Force in December 2022 , just before the COVID vaccine mandate was lifted by an act of Congress, 97.6 percent of the 490,000 members of the Active-Duty Air Force and Space Force, Air National Guard, and Air Force Reserve got fully vaccinated, leaving about 11,700 unvaccinated. The department noted approximately 1,080 religious and administration exemptions to the mandate at the time.

items.title: US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia
items.author: Reuters
items.summary: The U.S. Department of State said on Thursday it had approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.
items.body:
MilTech

US clears way for $24.3 billion fighter jet sale to Saudi Arabia

A U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II performs precision aerial maneuvers at Rickenbacker Air National Guard Base, Columbus, Ohio, June 19, 2026. (Airman Phyel Richardson/U.S. Air National Guard)

The U.S. Department of State said on Thursday it had approved the potential sale of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, as the kingdom is drawn deeper into war in the Middle East.

A sale would mark a significant policy shift from the U.S., potentially altering the balance of military power in the Middle East and testing Washington’s definition of maintaining its ally Israel’s “qualitative military edge.”

Saudi Arabia made a direct appeal for the jets in early 2025 to U.S. President Donald Trump and has long been interested in Lockheed Martin’s fighter.

The estimated $24.3 billion sale, which still needs congressional approval, would include 48 of the military aircraft and 49 Pratt & Whitney engines along with communications equipment, spare parts and other support items, the State Department said.

Washington weighs weapons sales to the Middle East in a way that ensures Israel maintains a “qualitative military edge”, effectively guaranteeing that Israel gets more advanced U.S. weapons than regional Arab states.

The Saudi embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, describing it as a further step in defense cooperation between the two countries.

“The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-U.S. strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defense cooperation,” the embassy said on X.

The F-35, built with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection, is considered the world’s most advanced fighter jet. Israel has operated the aircraft for a decade, building multiple squadrons, and remains the only Middle Eastern country to possess the system.

Saudi Arabia, the largest customer for U.S. arms, has sought the fighter for years as it looks to modernize its air force and counter regional threats, particularly from Iran. The kingdom’s renewed push for what would constitute two squadrons comes as the Trump administration has signaled openness to deepening defense cooperation with Riyadh. The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons.

The F-35 issue has also been intertwined with broader diplomatic efforts. The administration of former U.S. President Joe Biden previously explored providing F-35s to Saudi Arabia as part of a comprehensive deal that would have included Riyadh normalizing relations with Israel, though those efforts ultimately stalled.

Trump has made arms sales to Saudi Arabia a priority since returning to office. In 2025, the United States agreed to sell the kingdom an arms package worth nearly $142 billion, which the White House called “the largest defense cooperation agreement” Washington has ever done.

Congressional scrutiny could pose challenges to any F-35 sale. Lawmakers previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh following the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, and some members of Congress remain wary of deepening military cooperation with the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia is pursuing ambitious economic and military modernization plans under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 agenda. It has sought to diversify its defense partnerships while maintaining its decades-long security relationship with Washington.

items.title: Pentagon Picks 2 Companies for Reconnaissance Satellite Demo
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit have chosen two firms to demonstrate the ability of small satellites built with low-cost, commercial technology to track both friendly and adversary satellites in geosynchronous orbit. The post Pentagon Picks 2 Companies for Reconnaissance Satellite Demo appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit have chosen two firms to demonstrate the ability of small satellites built with low-cost, commercial technology to track both friendly and adversary satellites in geosynchronous orbit.

Northrop Grumman and True Anomaly will build prototype satellites for DIU’s GEO High-Resolution Optical Space-Based Tactical Reconnaissance, or GHOST-R, program, the Pentagon technology accelerator announced Sept. 18 in a LinkedIn post. The work will feed into a broader, multibillion dollar Space Force initiative called RG-XX, with the goal to begin fielding a fleet of reconnaissance satellites by the end of the decade.

Col. Bryon McClain, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power, said the Space Force is trying to “push the envelope” when it comes to both speed and affordability.

“This approach burns down technical risk, drives down lifecycle costs, and gets vital capability to the warfighter faster to ensure a more resilient architecture,” McClain said. “Successful prototypes will have a direct transition into the program of record.”

The Space Force in 2024 started talking about a lower-cost, commercial-based capability to augment its current fleet of Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program , or GSSAP, satellites. At the time, then-acting space acquisition executive Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy said the approach was partly motivated by a push from U.S. Space Command for more unclassified opportunities to partner with allies and industry.

It also aims to address two other SPACECOM needs: more maneuverable satellites and better space domain awareness to close gaps in its ability to characterize and track objects of concern in space. As recently as Sept. 16, Space Command Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting called for improved on-orbit targeting and tracking capabilities—and highlighted the fundamental role space domain awareness plays in the counterspace mission.

“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

In April, the Space Force chose 14 companies to be part of an industry consortium called Andromeda, where they’ll compete for task orders worth up to $6.2 billion. That contract will include work for both the maneuverable RG-XX reconnaissance satellites and a separate fleet of surveillance satellites called SG-XX.

As part of GHOST-R, Northrop and True Anomaly’s satellites are expected to launch in 2028 and then perform a series of demonstrations to prove they can collect high-resolution imagery and conduct weekly observations of target satellites. If successful, those spacecraft would become operational RG-XX platforms by 2029.

In parallel, the firms must provide a plan for scaling their satellites to a full constellation that can track all publicly catalogued objects in GEO.

Northrop, the incumbent prime contractor for GSSAP, said in a press release that its design will incorporate its ESPASat-L platform—a high-rate production bus—as well as optical payloads built by a company called TRL 11 based in Irvine, Calif.

“This award expands the company’s role in commercial, low-cost, proliferated space systems and builds on the success of the Northrop Grumman-built Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program,” the company said.

In its own statement, True Anomaly said it will leverage is Jackal spacecraft as well as its Mosaic ground system for GHOST-R.

“Jackal and Mosaic were purpose-built for this mission, delivering superior maneuverability, sensing, and autonomy at a price point that enables scale without compromising performance,” CEO Even Rogers said.

True Anomaly recently showcased its maneuverable Jackal spacecraft as part of the Space Force’s Victus Haze responsive space mission. During the mission, Jackal has demonstrated the ability to approach a target—in this case a satellite built by Rocket Lab—capture an image of it, characterize it, and “engage in a space-to-space pursuit” of the vehicle, the company said in a July statement.

Meanwhile, DIU recently posted another space-related solicitation , this time focused on fostering AI tools that can help distinguish between friendly objects and threats. The project, perhaps complementary to GHOST-R, seeks software that can “ingest and fuse massive streams of multi-source data,” like satellite imagery, geospatial data, and live video.

“By automating advanced cross-data correlation, the architecture aims to uncover hidden patterns, complex operational relationships, and predictive threat behaviors far beyond the capabilities of human analysis alone,” the solicitation states.

The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit, but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain.

Sept. 16, 2026

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

The Space Development Agency wants to wrap up its Tranche 1 launch campaign by the end of spring 2027, flying six more batches of satellites to build out its tracking and data transport constellations, according to Director Gurpartap Sandhoo.

Sept. 15, 2026

NASA is pushing hard to get astronauts back to the moon by 2028—and the urgency is driven in no small part by the national security implications of doing so before China does, Administrator Jared Isaacman said Sept. 15.

The Space Force estimates about 10 percent of its programs will be impacted under a continuing resolution for the coming fiscal year, according to Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess.

Guardians are playing a critical role in U.S. operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare effects to stifle enemy air defense and communication systems and other space capabilities vital to the war effort, Gen. Douglas Schiess said in one of his first appearances since swearing in as Chief of Space Operations.

Sept. 14, 2026

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed Sept. 14 the Space Force has “space control weapons” on orbit today—the Pentagon’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. is operating offensive capabilities in space.

Sept. 12, 2026

General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him? Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor…

items.title: US Air Force has a $14 billion supply hole, service officials say
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: As the force grapples with supply chain and maintenance issues, sustainment funding to fill the $14 billion gap is becoming increasingly necessary.
items.body:
MilTech

US Air Force has a $14 billion supply hole, service officials say

U.S. Air Force airmen upload an HH-60G Pave Hawk to be taken to the boneyard onto a C-17 Globemaster III at Aviano Air Base, Italy, July 15, 2024. (Jenna A. Bond/U.S. Air Force)

The U.S. Air Force has a $14 billion hole in supply for aircraft parts , affecting how the service acquires parts and looks at sustainment funding, service leaders said Wednesday.

As the force grapples with supply chain and maintenance issues as well as long aircraft service lives , sustainment funding is becoming increasingly necessary to bridge the gap, service officials said in a panel at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference .

“If I can throw a number out there right now, we have a $14 billion hole in supply,” Commander of Air Force Materiel Command Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry said during a panel titled “Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win.”

“Let that sink in for a minute,” she continued. “I know we’re not going to get it all at once, but when we get it, we’re going to have to execute. We’re going to have to execute smartly so we can move the needle.”

Hurry said that the service is managing the fleet more globally through partnerships, looking at parts with the Defense Logistics Agency and individual pieces that the force can get from the depot back in the field.

“From a supply perspective, our increase in the supply rate, or the number of aircraft that are down from a supply perspective, has increased 87% over the last seven years,” Hurry said.

On average, around 53% of the force’s fleet is over 30 years old, with 55% of the fleet over its “useful” service life, she said.

Hurry added that the force is working to receive additional funding for spare parts through advocating for the budget request to pass. In the fiscal year 2027 budget, the Department of the Air Force requested a record $338.8 billion , with $4.2 billion allotted for the Consolidated Sustainment Activity Group, or CSAG, that manages spare parts and maintenance backlogs, according to budget documents .

“But once we get even a penny, we have to be ready to execute it,” Hurry said.

Hurry also said that the service is striving to improve its “forecasting accuracy” to better understand where the needs are and where to position those assets globally by using artificial intelligence models and additive manufacturing.

On top of those measures, the service is putting long-term contracts in place that build stability in the collective supply chain and multiple sources of supply.

“Gone are the days of monopolies; we can’t just have one person producing the one critical part,” she said. “I need five [industry partners] producing them because if we get down to the crunch, we’re going to have to have a healthy shelf so that we can fight globally.”

The officials touted the North Star Readiness Campaign , which is meant to increase the number of mission-capable B-52 Stratofortress and B-1 Lancer aircraft by accelerating the delivery of parts, engineering support and depot maintenance.

The campaign has been the “number one driver” of improving readiness in the bomber fleet because of the supply increase the force has received, Gen. Stephen L. Davis, commander of the Air Force Global Strike Command, said during the panel.

Specifically, Davis said that the campaign has increased B-52 readiness by 40%.

“As a commander, you don’t want everything to be a money problem to solve it, but this I think is a money problem,” he said. “We need more money for parts. It’s absolutely the case.”

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.
